summary.text: The tenth substitution iterate has length at most \(4^{10}=1{,}048{,}576\), and all later positions have the default value \(1\), so the zero-position enumeration has already run out at \(n=1{,}048{,}577\) and the definition gives \(a(n)=1\). Since \(\sqrt3\ge0\), this makes \(n(3+\sqrt3)/3-a(n)>2\), furnishing a counterexample.

full_proof.text:
Let the substitution \(\sigma\) be
\[
\sigma(0)=01,\qquad \sigma(1)=0100.
\]
The formal statement under consideration constructs finite words
\[
L_0=0,\qquad L_{j+1}=\sigma(L_j),
\]
where substitution on a word means concatenating the substituted images of all its letters. It then uses only \(L_{10}\), extending that finite word by the symbol \(1\): if positions are numbered from \(0\), define
\[
w(k)=
\begin{cases}
\text{the symbol in position }k\text{ of }L_{10},&k<|L_{10}|,\\
1,&k\ge |L_{10}|.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus this \(w\) agrees with the beginning of the fixed point but, by definition, is constantly \(1\) after the end of the tenth iterate.

Let
\[
Z=\{k\in\mathbb N:w(k)=0\}.
\]
For a subset \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\), write \(E_S(j)\) for its \(j\)-th smallest element, with indexing beginning at \(0\). The enumeration convention in the statement is that if \(S\) has at most \(j\) elements, so that a \(j\)-th element does not exist, then
\[
E_S(j)=0.
\]
The sequence used in the conjecture is consequently
\[
a(n)=E_Z(n-1)+1.
\]
We will show that this definition gives \(a(1048577)=1\), after which the proposed estimate fails by an enormous margin.

First bound the length of the finite word. For every finite word \(L\),
\[
|\sigma(L)|\le 4|L|.
\]
Indeed, substitution of a concatenation is the concatenation of the substituted letters, so the length of \(\sigma(L)\) is the sum of the lengths of the substituted images of the letters of \(L\). There are three relevant cases for a letter in the formal rule: \(0\) has an image of length \(2\), \(1\) has an image of length \(4\), and any other natural-number symbol has the empty image, of length \(0\). In every case the image has length at most \(4\). Summing this inequality over the \(|L|\) letters proves the displayed bound.

It follows by induction that
\[
|L_j|\le 4^j
\]
for every \(j\ge0\). At \(j=0\), the word \(L_0=0\) has length \(1=4^0\). If \(|L_j|\le4^j\), then
\[
|L_{j+1}|=|\sigma(L_j)|\le4|L_j|\le4\cdot4^j=4^{j+1},
\]
which completes the induction. In particular,
\[
|L_{10}|\le4^{10}=1{,}048{,}576.
\]
Set
\[
N=1{,}048{,}576=4^{10}.
\]

If \(k\ge N\), then the length estimate gives \(k\ge |L_{10}|\). Such a \(k\) lies beyond the end of \(L_{10}\), so the default-extension definition gives \(w(k)=1\), not \(0\). Hence every zero position belongs to the finite interval from \(0\) through \(N-1\):
\[
Z\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}.
\]
That interval has exactly \(N\) elements. Therefore \(Z\) is finite and
\[
|Z|\le N.
\]
Consequently there cannot be an \(N\)-th element of \(Z\) under zero-based indexing: such an element would be the \((N+1)\)-st zero and would require at least \(N+1\) elements in \(Z\). By the stated default convention for the enumerating function,
\[
E_Z(N)=0.
\]

Now take
\[
n=N+1=1{,}048{,}577.
\]
Since \(n-1=N\), the definition of \(a\) yields
\[
a(1{,}048{,}577)=E_Z(1{,}048{,}577-1)+1
=E_Z(N)+1=0+1=1.
\]

It remains to compare this value with the proposed linear approximation. Put
\[
r=\frac{3+\sqrt3}{3}.
\]
Because \(\sqrt3\ge0\),
\[
r=1+\frac{\sqrt3}{3}\ge1.
\]
Therefore, for the positive integer \(n=1{,}048{,}577\),
\[
nr-a(n)=nr-1\ge n-1=1{,}048{,}576>2.
\]
In particular this quantity is positive, so its absolute value is itself, and hence
\[
\left|nr-a(n)\right|>2.
\]
Equivalently, the proposed upper inequality
\[
nr-a(n)<2
\]
already fails at \(n=1{,}048{,}577\). Thus it is false that every positive integer \(n\) satisfies
\[
-2<\frac{3+\sqrt3}{3}n-a(n)<2.
\]

The source of this counterexample is essential to the argument: the sequence in the accepted formal statement is defined from only the tenth substitution iterate and is filled with \(1\)'s afterward. It is therefore not the genuine infinite fixed point at arbitrarily large positions. Accordingly, the argument above disproves the universally quantified statement for the sequence definition used there; by itself it does not furnish a counterexample for the canonical infinite fixed point without that finite-prefix/default extension.
